title: Higher alcohols synthesis from syngas over lanthanum-promoted CuZnAl catalyst
abstract: CuZnAl catalysts with different La loadings were prepared by a complete liquid phase method and tested for higher alcohols (C2+OH) synthesis from syngas at the conditions of 250–290 °C, 4.5 MPa, feed low rate = 150 mL/min and H2/CO = 2. The catalysts were characterized by XRD, H2-TPR, NH3-TPD, N2 adsorption, XPS, and TEM techniques. Characterization results showed that the incorporation of La into CuZnAl catalysts resulted in the decrease of crystallite size of Cu0 and a strong interaction among copper and zinc or aluminum oxides. Especially, the incorporation of La increased the amount of weak acid and the Cu content on catalyst surface, which was speculated to contribute the formation of higher alcohols. Among these La-promoted CuZnAl catalysts, the La0.1 catalyst exhibited the best catalytic performance and the selectivity to higher alcohols reached above 60% when the reaction temperature was 290 °C.
paragraphs: The catalytic conversion of syngas (CO + H2) derived from coal, natural gas, or biomass into higher alcohols (C2+OH) has drawn much interest due to its potential use of alternative fuels and chemical feedstocks. Currently, several types of heterogeneous catalysts including noble metal Rh-based, modified Fischer–Tropsch synthesis catalysts and modified methanol synthesis catalysts (Cu-based) as well as hydrodesulfurization-type Mo-based catalysts are developed for C2+OH synthesis via CO hydrogenation. Among these catalysts, much less expensive Cu-based catalysts have become an attractive option.

As well known, CuZnAl catalyst is widely used for the conversion of syngas to methanol synthesis, which is an established, large-scale industrial process with the yield of methanol over 99%. Till now, there is still great number of publications focus on the active site of CuZnAl industrial catalyst for methanol synthesis. However, in our previous study, when the CuZnAl catalysts without promoters were prepared by a new preparation method named complete liquid phase method, ethanol was an unexpected product and the selectivity reached up to 40%. In order to reproduce the results, our group mainly focused on the absolutely same catalyst preparation condition or adding different promoters and even considering the influence of impurities in precursor to prepare CuZnAl catalyst via different students in past several years. Unfortunately, these methods were not effective. In contrast, the methanol selectivity became higher and higher, and even at last, the liquid product composed almost all of methanol, and the ethanol selectivity was even below 1%. Afterward, our group tried to change the preparation process of sol, it was surprising to found that the C2+OH selectivity increased significantly.

Lanthanum, always serving as either a promoter or a support, exhibits strong metal-support interactions, which can influence the catalytic activity. Furthermore, the application of lanthanum as a support or as a promoter in the synthesis of higher alcohols over traditional CuCo-based catalysts has also been reported. For example, Lebarbier et al. investigated higher alcohols synthesis from syngas over La2O3-promoted cobalt catalysts, and the characterization results showed that the presence of La would greatly influence the amount of Co2C which favored the couple of CO and CH x to form a CC bond. Wu et al. found that the introduction of La promoter to K-Cu/ZrO2 catalyst not only facilitated the dispersion of CuO, but also improved Cu–Zr interaction, which resulted the higher selectivity to C2+OH and catalytic activity of CO hydrogenation. Adachi et al. reported that the addition of La could promote the activity of Co/SiO2 catalysts by the agglomeration of cobalt.

In this study here, a series of La-promoted CuZnAl catalysts are synthesized and tested for CO hydrogenation. The purpose of the present work is to study the promotional effects of La2O3 in the synthesis of higher alcohols from syngas. And the catalysts were characterized by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), N2 adsorption–desorption, H2 temperature programmed reduction (H2-TPR), NH3 temperature-programmed desorption (NH3-TPD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

The CuZnAl catalysts with different La loadings were prepared by a complete liquid phase method. The process was divided into two steps: sol preparation and liquid phase heat treatment process. In the first step, aluminum isopropoxide (C3H7O)3Al was hydrolyzed in 100 mL deionized water dissolving a certain amount of citric acid at 50 °C for 3 h, then the bath temperature was raised up to 95 °C and kept for 0.5 h. Next, a mixed solution of Cu(NO3)2•3H2O, Zn(NO3)2•6H2O, and La(NO3)3•6H2O dissolved in glycol was slowly added into the above Al solution. At last, the resulting CuZnAl solution was stirred at 95 °C until a homogeneous sol was obtained. The sol was then aged for 10 days at ambient temperature to obtain gel. The second step was the preparation of CuZnAl slurry catalysts. The gel was dispersed in liquid paraffin, heated under N2 atmosphere from ambient temperature to 300 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min and kept at 300 °C for 8 h, then a slurry catalyst was subsequently obtained. In this paper, the undoped CuZnAl catalyst was denoted as La0, the La doped CuZnAl catalysts were assigned as Lax, where “x” was the molar ratios of Cu:Zn:Al:La = 2:1:0.8:x.
Before characterization, the slurry catalysts were centrifuged, extracted using petroleum ether to remove the adsorbed liquid paraffin and dried at ambient temperature to obtain the solid samples.
XRD data of samples were collected on a Rigaku D/MAX-2500 diffractometer equipped with Ni mono-chromator and Cu Kα (40 kV, 100 mA) radiation.
The textural properties of samples were measured by N2 adsorption at −196 °C on a Micromeritics Quanta chrome instrument.

TPR experiments were carried out with 50 mg of sample in a quartz reactor using 5% H2/N2 gaseous mixture. The temperature was increased from ambient temperature to 500 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min, and H2 consumption was recorded using a calibrated thermal conductivity detector.

NH3-TPD experiments were measured after previous reduction of the fresh samples. First, the pretreated samples were saturated with pure NH3 at 50 °C for 30 min. After subsequent flushing for 30 min in He flow to remove all the physically adsorbed molecules, TPD data were collected from 50 to 480 °C with a heating rate of 10 °C/min.

XPS experiments were performed on an ESCALAB 250 spectrometer (VG Scientific Ltd., UK) equipped with Al Kα radiation (hυ = 1486.6 eV) under ultrahigh vacuum (10–7 Pa). The binding energies were calibrated internally by an adventitious carbon deposit C (1 s).
TEM images were taken with a JEOL JEM-2999FMII apparatus. Samples were dispersed in ethanol, sonicated for 20 min, and then deposited over a Formvar copper grid to be observed in the microscope.

The catalytic reactions were carried out using 0.5 L slurry bed reactor with continuous mechanical agitator. About 20 g of slurry catalyst was not pre-reduced by hydrogen before each catalytic reaction. The catalytic evaluation was carried out in the reactor by directly introducing syngas (H2/CO = 2, v/v) under 250–290 °C, 4.5 MPa with a feed flow rate of 150 mL/min. All the data were collected at least 24 h before reaction. The exit gas was analyzed online by a column of TDX-01 and a thermal conductivity detector TCD regarding H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, while CH x mixtures were analyzed by a column of GDX-502 and a flame ionization detector, respectively. The liquid products were collected daily and analyzed offline using the same device. The correction factor of each product was first calculated, then the CO conversion and the carbon-based selectivities to CO2, hydrocarbons, dimethyl ether and C2+OH were calculated by an internal normalization method as follows: Conversion for CO ( % ) : X CO = F in · V CO in − F out · V CO out F in · V CO in × 100 % Selectivity to C 2 + OH ( % ) = Quantity of C 2 + OH Total quantity of products × 100 % where F in and F out were the inlet and outlet flow rates, which were calculated by the mass flowmeter and wet flowmeter respectively. V CO in and V CO out were the CO volume fractions of feed gas and outlet gas.

The XRD patterns of CuZnAl catalysts with different La loadings were shown in Fig. 1 . As shown, the weak diffraction peak of 2θ at 35.6° was ascribed to ZnO phase. The strong peaks at 2θ = 43.3°, 50.4°, and 74.1° were assigned to the (111), (200), and (220) reflections of Cu0 crystalline phase. No CuO or Cu2O phase was observed, this was possible due to the part decomposition of liquid paraffin, which was then formed free carbon, and thus causing the generation of Cu0. It could be seen that the peak intensity of Cu0 in La0.1 catalyst showed a significant decrease compared with that of La0 catalyst and further decreased with the increase of La content, which meant that the crystallite size of Cu0 was strongly affected after the addition of La. This observation was also reflected on the size of Cu0 particles in the materials calculated using the Scherrer equation (Table 1 ). One could see that the average size of Cu0 was about 33.5 nm for La0 catalyst, it was then decreased to 32.0 nm for La0.1 sample and further decreased to 29.8 nm for La0.2 sample. The relative size decreasing ratio was calculated about 4.4% and 6.9%, respectively. However, the diffraction lines of Al species could not be observed for all the catalysts, this was most probably due to the relative lower Al content which was below the detection limit of XRD, since the Al species was generally formed as AlOOH phase when the catalysts were prepared by the complete liquid phase method.

TPR measurements were performed to investigate the reduction behavior of the catalysts. As observed in Fig. 2 , all the catalysts exhibited only a reduction peak in the temperature range of 100–400 °C, which was attributed to the reduction of Cu+ species. Meanwhile, it was clearly seen that the reduction peak shifted to higher temperature, indicating that Cu2O species could be reduced more difficultly to metallic Cu after La added, which suggested that the existence of La caused a strong interaction among copper and zinc or aluminum oxides. Moreover, one could see that the peak intensity enhanced after the addition of La, and more obviously for La0.2 catalyst, revealing that the amount of reducible Cu2O in La0.2 catalyst was greater than that of other two catalysts and the addition of La was beneficial to the dispersion of Cu, which was consistent with the following TEM results.

NH3-TPD measurements were carried out in order to monitor the acid strength and the amount of acid sites of the catalyst surface prior to HAS. The acidity was believed to significantly influence the efficiency of CO hydrogenolysis. As observed in Fig. 3 , the profiles of all the catalysts showed a single peak of NH3 desorption at about 110 °C and this weak acid site was ascribed to the weak interactions that occurred between NH3 and OH groups of the oxides. It also could be found that the intensity of peak increased after the addition of La, indicating that the existence of La would increase the amount of weak acid on catalyst surface. Several works had demonstrated that OH groups played a crucial role in C2+OH synthesis. And in this study, Al species mainly existed in AlOOH phase which had sufficient OH groups and was considered as the main reason for surface weak acid. Thus, combined with the following activity results, it was speculated that a relative larger amount of weak acid favored the formation of C2+OH.

Fig. 4 presented the nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms and the corresponding pore size distributions of different catalysts. It could be seen from Fig. 4(a) that all the catalysts exhibited a typical IV isotherm with an H1-type hysteresis loop, this type of hysteresis loop indicated the existence of mesoporous. The mesopore size distributions of different catalysts were calculated by the Barrett–Joyne–Halenda (BJH) model. The La0 catalyst possessed two kinds of mesopores, whereas La-promoted catalysts had only a very narrow pore size distribution with a pronounced peak at about 4 nm. More detailed textural properties are shown in Table 2 . It was observed that the addition of La decreased the BET surface area before reaction, and after reaction, the BET surface area of all the catalysts increased. This was a universal phenomenon for the catalyst prepared by a complete liquid phase method which would cause a small amount of liquid paraffin adsorbed in the pore of catalyst, during the reaction, this adsorbed liquid paraffin was then gradually removed out, then the surface area greatly increased. However, we could not find any correlation between the textural properties of catalysts and their catalytic activities.

The surface composition and the chemical states of Cu, Zn, Al and La on catalysts surface were determined by XPS experiments and displayed in Fig. 5 and Table 3 . The measurements revealed the absence of Cu2+ species on the catalysts surface since the Cu 2p 3/2 and the Cu 2p 1/2 peaks were centered at about 932 eV and 952 eV, respectively (Fig. 5a). Furthermore, no obvious satellite peaks were observed between 940 and 945 eV. Also, it could be seen that the binding energy (B.E.) value of Cu 2p 3/2 increased slightly (Table 3) after La added, which suggested that the addition of La might favor to increase the proportion of Cuδ+on catalyst surface. However, since the XAES peaks of the three catalysts were widely dispersed (Fig. 5b), and the concentration of Cu species on catalyst surface was too low to be detected, so it was difficult to differentiate the Cu+ and Cu0 species. In addition, as observed in Table 3 and Fig. 6( a), the B.E. of Zn 2p 3/2 located at about 1021.5 eV could be attributed to the reported data of Zn2+. These results were in consistent with XRD analysis. The Al 2p peak was located in the range of 73.8–74.5 eV (Fig. 6b), corresponding to AlOH bonds, which was ascribed to the octahedral AlO6 of AlOOH.

Surface compositions of the catalysts were calculated and presented in Table 3. Compared with the feed ratio of the bulk catalysts (Cu: Zn: Al = 2:1:0.8), it was found that the surface of catalyst was considerably depleted of Cu. In contrast, an enrichment of Zn and Al on the surface was observed. Meanwhile, it could be seen from Table 3 that the Cu/Zn and Cu/Al ratios increased after the addition of La, and the La0.1 catalyst possessed the biggest values. Combined with the following activity results, it was suggested that higher Cu content on catalyst surface might favored the formation of higher alcohols.

The particle size and elemental dispersions of the catalysts were investigated by TEM analyses. As seen in Fig. 7 , the Cu nano-particles (dark area) in La0 sample could be easily distinguished in TEM images and their size in diameters was found to be in the range of 20–100 nm. After the addition of La, the Cu dispersion increased and Cu nano-particles were intimate contact with the surrounding Zn and Al, revealing that the well dispersed Cu nano-particles were embedded in the amorphous alumina. Thus, it was hard to measure the particle size of Cu from TEM images. However, it was obviously seen that both the size of Cu particles and elemental dispersions in CuZnAl samples were strongly affected after La addition, which might one reason for different catalytic performance.

The overall catalytic performance of different catalysts toward CO hydrogenation to higher alcohols was summarized in Tables 4 and 5 . One could see that CO conversion first increased and then decreased with the increase of La content, and the La0.1 catalyst showed the maximum value, In addition, it was found that the relationship between C2+OH selectivity showed the similar tendency as that of the CO conversion. These results suggested that a small number of La favored the formation of C2+OH, while an excess of La would promote methanol formation. Moreover, it was observed that the dimethyl ether (DME) selectivity exhibited the inverse tendency with the selectivity to C2+OH, which suggested that they were controlled by the opposite active center.

The catalytic performance of La0.1 catalyst at different temperature and with time on stream at 290 °C was shown in Fig. 8 . It could be seen from Fig. 8(a) that the temperature had little effect on CO conversion and the total alcohols selectivity. This was probably due to the special catalyst preparation method, which would produce a certain amount of free carbon on the surface of metal. To some extent, this kind of free carbon would inhibit the improvement of catalyst activity. However, the ethanol and C2+OH selectivity increased with the increase of temperature, and it almost increased linearly above 270 °C, which suggested that raising temperature favored the formation of higher alcohols. This might probably due to that higher temperature ( > 270 °C) facilitated the cleavage of CO bonds or possible equilibrium of methanol synthesis was reached at relatively higher temperature in the reaction system. Obviously, there was no deactivation at different temperatures in the first stage. Nonetheless, in the second stage, it could be seen from Fig. 8(b) that the selectivity of ethanol and C2+OH slightly decreased to 25% and 50% after 194 h reaction, respectively. This was mainly due to that the Al components existed in the form of AlOOH which was an unstable phase at relative higher temperature and it was believed to play an important role in C2+OH synthesis from syngas according to our previous experimental and theoretical studies.

Fig. 9 presented the Anderson–Schulz–Flory (logarithm of mole fraction vs. carbon number) plots of alcohols and hydrocarbons over La0.1 catalyst at 290 °C. As shown, the carbon number distributions of alcohols and hydrocarbons did not meet the linear A–S–F distribution on the catalysts. It was clear observed that methanol showed a negative deviation and methane showed a positive deviation from the ASF behavior, which suggested that alcohols and hydrocarbons might derive from the same intermediates. This was similar with traditional CuCo or CuFe-based mixed alcohols synthesis catalysts. Obviously, Fe and Co elements were not indispensable for higher alcohols synthesis from syngas.

Fig. 10 displayed the estimated chain growth factors of alcohols and hydrocarbons over La0.1 catalyst at different temperatures. It could be seen that the chain growth probability of both alcohols and hydrocarbons increased with the increase of temperature. This meant the chain growth ability of the catalyst increased with the increase of temperature. Similar change trends of chain growth factors of alcohols and hydrocarbons further indicated that alcohols and hydrocarbons derived from the same intermediates.

In conclusion, the introduction of La promoter into CuZnAl catalyst had an obvious influence on the physicochemical properties and catalytic performance of higher alcohols synthesis from CO hydrogenation. The introduction of La promoter into CuZnAl catalyst not only decreased the crystallite size of Cu0 species, but also enhanced a strong interaction among copper and zinc or aluminum oxides. It was also concluded that adding La into the catalysts increased the amount of weak acid and Cu content on catalyst surface, which was speculated to contribute the formation of higher alcohols. Comparing with CuZnAl catalyst and other La-promoted CuZnAl catalysts, the La0.1 catalyst exhibited the best catalytic performance. In addition, raising temperature favored the formation of higher alcohols and the selectivity to higher alcohols reached above 60% over La0.1 catalyst when the reaction temperature was 290 °C. Moreover, it was speculated that alcohols and hydrocarbons might derive from the same intermediates.
